title: Not a Draw: Keep the King Away from the Corner
summary: A wrong-colored bishop and rook pawn can still win when coordinated barriers prevent the defending king reaching the promotion corner.

nodes.question: Should Black push the pawn or improve the bishop?
nodes.explanation: Black has Ke6, Be3 and h3 against White Kf3. It is Black to move. The bishop has the wrong color for h1, but White has not yet reached the corner.

branches.title: Build the bishop-and-pawn barrier
commentary: Black has Ke6, Be3 and h3 against White Kf3. It is Black to move. The bishop has the wrong color for h1, but White has not yet reached the corner.
Bf4 offers the bishop while blocking White’s approach through g3. Pawn h3 denies g2, so the king cannot slip toward h1.
Kf2 stays near the corner without taking the bishop. This is the illustrated defensive retreat.

Bh2 establishes the final barrier. The bishop controls g1/g3 while h3 controls g2. The exact position is winning for Black; the later king approach still needs accurate play and is not encoded as an immediate promotion.
branches.explanation: Bh2 establishes the final barrier. The bishop controls g1/g3 while h3 controls g2. The exact position is winning for Black; the later king approach still needs accurate play and is not encoded as an immediate promotion.

branches.title: Independent early pawn push permits the corner
commentary: Black has Ke6, Be3 and h3 against White Kf3. It is Black to move. The bishop has the wrong color for h1, but White has not yet reached the corner.
h2 gives up the win. The pawn stops controlling g2, opening a route for the defending king.
Kg2 uses the newly available square. White preserves the exact draw.
Bg1 is an independently selected representative continuation. The bishop cannot control h1 because it moves on the other color.
Kh1 reaches the drawing corner. Black cannot force promotion with this wrong-colored bishop and rook pawn; the exact result is a draw.

branches.explanation: Kh1 reaches the drawing corner. Black cannot force promotion with this wrong-colored bishop and rook pawn; the exact result is a draw.

branches.title: Taking the offered bishop loses the pawn race
commentary: Black has Ke6, Be3 and h3 against White Kf3. It is Black to move. The bishop has the wrong color for h1, but White has not yet reached the corner.
Bf4 can be offered because the pawn supplies a second threat.
Kxf4 removes the bishop but leaves the king too far from the h-pawn.
h2 advances one step from promotion. White cannot get to h1 in one move.
Kg3 tries to approach, but cannot stop the immediate promotion. This legal representative reply is independently selected.
h1=Q promotes. The resulting queen-versus-king position is exactly winning for Black; its later conversion is outside this branch.

exercises.prompt: Why is the wrong-colored bishop not automatically a draw?
exercises.answer: The familiar draw requires the defending king to reach h1. Here Black can deny g1, g2 and g3 with the bishop and pawn, then bring the king closer.

exercises.prompt: Why does pushing h2 too soon fail?
exercises.answer: It removes the pawn’s control of g2. White can use that square to reach h1 before Black builds the barrier.

startContext: Begin after White Kf3 at 110s, with Black Ke6/Be3/h3. The four-piece position is reconstructed from the saved physical-board diagrams and adjacent frames. Bf4/Kf2/Bh2 is the illustrated barrier. The early-push and bishop-capture continuations use independently selected representative replies. Earlier ...Be3 and ...h3 decisions are source context.
